entries.title: Fossil fuel talks deadlock pushes COP31 climate summit into overtime
entries.summary: EU warns COP31 risks turning into a 'fossil summit' as critical climate commitments are omitted from the draft deal.
entries.content:
EU warns COP31 risks turning into a ‘fossil summit’ as critical climate commitments are omitted from the draft deal.

The COP31 climate summit has gone into overtime as nearly 200 countries remain deadlocked over a draft deal that no longer mentions fossil fuels.

The two-week talks in Antalya, Turkiye, were due to end on Friday, when a late closing session approved some technical matters, but not the wider political deal.

“We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet,” COP31 President and Turkiye’s Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates.

Environmental groups tracking the two-week conference said the meeting lacked ambition to address the ‌worsening climate crisis and was on track to be the “worst COP ever”.

A third draft is expected on Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.

The fossil fuel fight

An opening draft from cohost and lead negotiator Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected.

Oil producers have also resisted similar language at past talks, including at COP28 in 2023. The revised text also dropped a $120bn target for money to help poorer countries adapt to climate change.

The European Union said the draft “risks turning this climate COP into a fossil summit”. Panama, which signed a letter with a dozen other countries demanding “a clear transition away from fossil fuels”, threatened to walk away from the talks.

“It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it,” Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, told a news conference.

Other contested points

The draft proposes raising the share of the world’s final energy consumption that comes from electricity to 35 percent by 2035. It does not say the power must come from renewables, and some countries want the target to say “clean”.

Some countries also reject a push to expand carbon capture, a technology that traps emissions from power plants and factories. They say it is costly and unproven, and could let polluters keep burning oil and gas.

“We want to see the references to false solutions removed,” said Vanuatu’s climate minister, Ralph Regenvanu.

Developing countries are angry that rich nations are falling short on climate finance. “We didn’t come here to beg,” said Ghana’s environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings.

Tough backdrop

A UN report last month found the world is set to pass the 1.5-degree-Celsius (2.7F) warming limit set under the 2015 Paris Agreement.

The United States, the largest historical emitter, is absent for a second year after President Donald Trump ended climate cooperation.

The US-Israel war on Iran and higher living costs have also drawn attention away from the talks.

Environmental groups say the summit lacks ambition.

“This has been the worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the think tank Power Shift Africa.

entries.title: US lawmakers push for tougher AI chip rules amid China export crackdown
entries.summary: Washington has new rules restricting remote access to advanced US AI chips, but lawmakers want more.
entries.content:
Washington has new rules restricting remote access to advanced US AI chips, but lawmakers want more.

United States lawmakers say more regulations are needed to protect advanced AI chips once they leave the country, even as they support the recently imposed chip export controls.

This week, the US Department of Commerce announced a new rule to restrict how advanced US AI chips can be accessed remotely in the wake of the previous Nvidia CEO’s affair with a suspected spy for Beijing. The move would close what officials described as a loophole that allows Chinese companies to tap into computing power through data centres in third countries, bypassing US restrictions.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which sits under the Commerce Department, said the rule would require data centre customers in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Brazil to apply for a special licence to buy advanced chips from US companies, including Nvidia, because they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion”.

“The export controls should have been in place, certainly,” Democratic Representative Pramila Jayapal told Al Jazeera. “I also think it’s a bigger conversation about who dominates the AI market. We should not have this consolidation of all the AI knowledge in a couple of companies because that poses an enormous threat on multiple levels, including national security.”

In October, Jayapal introduced a policy framework that would require every AI company operating in the US to obtain a federal charter in an effort to protect the public interest.

The AI charter, the framework says, is modelled after existing regulatory frameworks, combining the round-the-clock federal oversight, strict safety mandates, and structural separation built into national bank charters with the rigorous pre-release federal testing required for nuclear materials and dangerous weapons.

The framework also bans AI companies from building empires, releasing risky models, stealing through surveillance, exploiting workers, or causing harm.

Lutnick probe

Jayapal is a member of the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee, whose ranking members announced a probe to determine whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China.

Lutnick is facing criticism, including from members of US President Donald Trump’s cabinet, for allegedly refusing to impose restrictions on companies accused of diverting advanced chips to China, including Megaspeed, which is at the centre of the Nvidia probe.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee also announced that the Trump administration had approved exports of 879,000 chips manufactured by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026.

Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress in January, expressed a desire to better limit chip exports amid growing scrutiny over the extent to which US computing power may have reached China.

“I’m excited to get these gavels and go through the investigatory work that’s necessary, but also to rein in and regulate artificial intelligence. The very industry is asking to be regulated by Congress,” Democratic Representative Everton Blair told Al Jazeera.

‘Tremendous penalties’

The US accounts for nearly 75 percent of the world’s AI spending and computing power, followed by China.

US tech giants, including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, operate nearly 90 major AI computing hubs globally, according to an Oxford University study. The same research found that US companies were building 63 AI computing hubs outside the country as of 2025.

Stephen Ezell, vice president for global innovation policy at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF), said Washington would find it difficult to enforce the BIS rule.

China has rejected the restriction, calling it “economic coercion” by the US.

On Friday, after his return to the White House from his historic trilateral meeting with the Chinese and Russian presidents in Shenzhen, China, Trump promised to prohibit US companies from developing data centres in other countries.

“We’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” Trump said.

It was unclear what Trump had envisioned, or how he would enforce it.

At the same time, he urged Americans to embrace data centres in their neighbourhoods, despite communities’ increasing concern about the centres’ impact on quality of life, environment and energy demands.

Analysts say the recent export regulation has likely not had much effect on China’s efforts to become the global leader in AI semiconductor chips.

“China does not want to depend upon American or other foreign semiconductors. They want to develop them themselves, and one can argue that we’ve slowed them down a little bit with our export controls, but in no way has it changed China’s aspirations to become the global AI semiconductor chip leader,” Ezell said on Al Jazeera’s This Is America.

entries.title: Trump defends Putin relationship, warns AI data centres must stay in US
entries.summary: The US president also spoke about the war in Iran and praised trip to China during a wide-ranging news conference.
entries.content:
The US president also spoke about the war in Iran and praised trip to China during a wide-ranging news conference.

United States President Donald Trump has praised his recent trip to China and defended the relationship with his “friend” Vladimir Putin, but questioned whether the Russian president was a friend to the US.

On Friday, during a White House news briefing, Trump was asked about the “friend” remark — made during his historic summit with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this week — and whether the Russian leader was a friend to the US.

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump told reporters before saying Putin had been “very nice” during what he described as the “Russia hoax” investigation after his 2016 presidential campaign.

“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship. And it’s actually very good,” Trump added as he talked about Russia’s nuclear weapons capabilities.

“I think it gives us a lot of additional strength,” he said.

Trump also spoke about the historic nature of his meeting with Xi and Putin, praising the “first of its kind trilateral peace agreement”.

“We had one of the most momentous international summits in many years. That was the first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China,” Trump said.

No major deals were announced from the summit. But Trump, on Friday, played up his agreement with the two leaders to hold future discussions on nuclear proliferation.

The US president’s remarks came during a wide-ranging news conference, where topics from Iran to artificial intelligence were also discussed.

Trump accused Iran of negotiating in bad faith to end the war, which is about to mark its 10-month anniversary.

“They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me,” he said. “We wanna make a real deal, not a fake deal.”

Trump added: “They’ve been b*********** people for 51 years.”

During the news conference, US Vice President JD Vance and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both possible 2028 presidential contenders, flanked Trump in the White House press briefing room.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Defence Secretary Hegseth, as well as newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, were also present.

Trump denied he was upset at Vance for blaming US Republicans’ historic midterm losses on the Iran war, saying, “People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion.”

“I thought his statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that, if we were asked, I would have said that, would you do it again, and absolutely the answer is yes,” Trump said. “I saw that, but no problem there at all.”

No data centres abroad

Vance was asked by reporters about his thoughts on his party’s midterm drubbing.

“I think the president is the one who makes the decision. And the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said. “My goal, in my job, is to support the President of the United States.”

Trump also warned US tech companies against building new artificial intelligence data centres overseas. Otherwise, he said, they will face a “tremendous tax”.

“We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them”, Trump said. “And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

Trump did not provide details on how he would enforce such a policy and said he had not yet told his own officials about his plan.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment but has not yet heard back.

entries.title: Two Salvadoran soldiers killed in Haiti while handling explosives
entries.summary: Two others were injured in the explosion, marking the first deaths among troops deployed to Haiti since late October.
entries.content:
Two others were injured in the explosion, marking the first deaths among troops deployed to Haiti since late October.

Two Salvadoran soldiers have been killed in Haiti while handling explosive material, El Salvador’s army said, marking the first deaths among the roughly 2,500 troops who have been deployed to the country since late October.

Two others were injured in the explosion at one of the camps and are receiving medical care, the army said in a post on X on Friday. It did not reveal the identities of the soldiers.

The deaths come just over a month after El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele sent troops into Haiti, announcing a rescue mission to find four aviation technicians who went missing on October 18 after an attack on their vehicle near the capital, Port-au-Prince.

They were working with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) at the time.

The rescue mission has since broadened into an offensive against Haiti’s gangs, with Salvadoran soldiers working alongside Haitian and international forces.

Salvadoran officials have said they plan to leave once the four missing technicians are found.

Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, told The Associated Press news agency earlier this month that the men were dead, although he provided no evidence. El Salvador’s government maintains they are alive.

The Haitian government has suggested it wants the deployment to be extended, and some Haitians took to the streets in Haiti and elsewhere earlier this week in large rallies to express support for the troops and Bukele.

The terms of the bilateral agreement between Haiti and El Salvador have not been revealed publicly, but according to the UN, most Salvadoran soldiers are operating outside the GSF and do not fall under the UN’s reporting mechanism for that mission.

Bukele has been promoting the intervention on social media, posting videos of strikes on homes belonging to gang leaders, and Haitian officials announced earlier this week that they retook control of the national football stadium.

Analysts, however, have questioned how much the Salvadoran deployment has contributed to recent gains and whether those gains would last.

They have also raised concerns about the risk to civilians, citing a lack of transparency around the rules of engagement and how Salvadoran troops are monitored.

On Thursday, Bukele officially launched his bid for a third presidential term. The elections are scheduled for February.

entries.title: Sudan’s war leaves disabled children missing out on education
entries.summary: War forces schools, rehabilitation centres to close, forcing children with disabilities to lose access to education.
entries.content:
War forces schools, rehabilitation centres to close, forcing children with disabilities to lose access to education.

Khartoum, Sudan – Four-year-old Muzan Abdelrahman should be preparing to start her educational journey. But she has a hearing impairment, and in Sudan, a country devastated by war, the specialised support she needs to attend school is not available.

When conflict broke out in April 2023, Muzan was only a few months old. Many hoped that the war between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces would be over by now, and Muzan could grow up in an environment where she could get the assistance she needs.

Instead, the war has dragged on, with no end in sight and a humanitarian crisis consuming the country. For Muzan, that means the specialised education and rehabilitation centres she relies on have closed.

“My daughter needs training and continuous follow-up at this age. I try to help her at home, but I am not a specialist and cannot provide the rehabilitation sessions or educational tools she needs,” Muzan’s mother, Abeer Osman, told Al Jazeera. “What frightens me most is that these important years will pass without her getting the opportunity to learn how to communicate and express herself.”

The family’s experience is not isolated. Across Sudan, children with disabilities face obstacles to education and support as institutions are destroyed and families are displaced.

For 14-year-old Mohammed Ahmed, who has a physical disability, getting to school is a challenge, but so is moving around once he arrives. Inaccessible entrances and staircases leave him dependent on others.

“I want to continue my education like the rest of my classmates, but I struggle to reach classrooms and move between them,” Ahmed told Al Jazeera. “What frustrates me most is that I want to learn, but the school environment does not always make that possible.”

“I do not want my disability to deprive me of education or limit my future opportunities,” he added. “I want a school where I can access classrooms and facilities independently and with dignity.”

Generation locked out of education

The war is restricting access to schooling for children across Sudan.

According to UNICEF, at least 8 million school-age children lack access to formal education. As of August, about 30 percent of the country’s schools were not operational, with around 1 percent being used as shelters for displaced people.

But the issue is particularly acute for children with disabilities.

Before the war, Sudan had more than 230 schools for disabled children, according to figures from the UN children’s agency. Many have since closed, although the exact number is uncertain, with no up-to-date information available. Al Jazeera reached out to the Sudanese government for comment, but had not received a response at the time of publishing.

Aisha Abbo remembers the services her son, eight-year-old Ali Hassan, had access to before the war.

Ali, who has Down’s syndrome, used to attend a school for children with disabilities before the war, and received support to develop academic, communication, and social skills.

Those services were provided by the government, but now the same facilities are shut, and private centres are simply too expensive.

“When the war broke out in Khartoum, we could no longer afford to continue his education,” Aisha told Al Jazeera. “We are calling on the government to pay attention to children with disabilities, reopen specialised centres and provide the teachers, specialists, and programmes they need. These children cannot wait until the war ends and life returns to normal. Every day without education or training affects their development and abilities.”

In Khartoum, the impact is clear at the Usratuna Sudanese Association for Children with Disabilities, whose facilities were partly hit by shelling at the start of the war more than three-and-a-half years ago. A projectile struck its classrooms, while damage to buildings and the loss of equipment have made it harder to resume activities.

Badr al-Din Tawfiq, the association’s project manager and representative of its director, said most rehabilitation and support services had stopped because of the war, funding shortages and damage to its facilities.

“At present, we are unable to provide most of our services. We receive children’s registrations and collect their information, but we cannot respond to families’ requests because funding is unavailable. The premises need rehabilitation, the classrooms are unsafe, and we do not have the equipment needed to run rehabilitation programmes,” he told Al Jazeera.

Tawfiq said the association had registered more than 100 children for physiotherapy, speech therapy, behavioural support and vocational rehabilitation. Families had also requested hearing aids and batteries.

“So far, we have been unable to provide the services families are requesting. There are no tools or equipment, and we have not been able to resume our work as it was before the war,” he said.

Rebuilding services

Some activities that do not require funding, including psychosocial support and advocacy, remain possible. The association’s inclusive kindergarten in Dar al-Salam, Omdurman, also continues to operate. But most of its other activities in Khartoum have stopped, while its branches in Zalingei, in central Darfur, and Blue Nile state are no longer operating.

Nagi Mansour, director-general of the Sudanese Coalition for Education for All, said the education of children with disabilities had faced significant challenges even before the war.

“The main problems included poor infrastructure, a shortage of specialised schools and qualified teachers, and a lack of adapted curricula, Braille materials and sign-language teaching resources,” he told Al Jazeera.

Mansour said the war had compounded the problems, closing or destroying institutions, displacing families and depriving some students of assistive devices.

He called for a national survey to identify children who had dropped out of education and assess their needs. He also urged the rehabilitation of special education centres, the provision of appropriate educational materials, Braille resources and sign-language interpreters, and training for teachers in inclusive education.

“Children with disabilities have an inherent right to education. They are not simply a group receiving humanitarian assistance. The rebuilding of education in Sudan must be based on justice, equity and inclusive education to ensure that no child is left behind because of their needs or the circumstances of war and displacement,” he said.
